claim: Zionism is a colonial project that stole the land.

heard.who: Rashid Khalidi, historian, in a 2024 interview
heard.quote: one of the major institutions that was involved in taking over land from Palestinians

answer: Before 1948 Jews bought land; they did not seize it. By the Mandate government's own count Jewish-owned land was about 1.5 to 1.7 million dunams, roughly 6 to 7 percent of the country (the total includes desert and state land). Most purchases were from large landowners, many of them absentee, and a Jewish National Fund policy held the land as the Jewish people's inalienable property. But the sales cost Arab tenant farmers their holdings: in 1930 the Hope Simpson report found that of 688 farming families on land bought in the Jezreel valley, 309 had joined the landless. The Shaw Commission and the British appointed official then examined the landlessness, and in 1940 Britain restricted sales. Historians dispute how many were displaced and who was to blame.

facts.text: Purchases from large owners cost Arab tenant farmers their holdings. In 1930 the Hope Simpson report found that of 688 Arab families who farmed villages in the Jezreel (Esdraelon) valley bought by Jewish buyers, only 379 still farmed and 309 had joined the landless classes; the government's own officers counted 1,270 farmers displaced from those villages.

facts.text: The 1939 White Paper gave the High Commissioner powers 'to prohibit and regulate transfers of land'; the Land Transfer Regulations of 1940 divided the country into zones, banning or restricting land sales to Jews in the zones that covered 95 percent of the area. Jewish buyers largely got around them.

contested.text: Whether the land was bought or taken depends on the period. Khalidi describes the Jewish Colonization Agency as taking over land from Palestinians. Stein, an American historian, finds the core of the future state was bought from willing Arab sellers, many of them leading Arab politicians. Both agree on the facts that purchases happened and tenants were displaced; they differ on blame.

sources.quote: The lands which became the critical core for Israel were provided by Arab sellers.

contested.text: How many tenants were displaced is disputed. Hope Simpson's officers counted 1,270 farmers displaced from the Esdraelon villages. Stein says that on the 200,000 dunams of Sursock land fewer than 700 Arab tenants worked, perhaps 5,000 people in all, and that other large purchases, such as the Wadi Hawarith, displaced more.

could_not_verify: The Shaw Commission's own words on a 'landless and discontented class' appear on a scholarly page (Charles Anderson, Middle Eastern Studies) that I could not read here; I did not quote them.
Lewis French's reports (1931-32) are described only by their terms of reference in the Mandate government's Survey of Palestine; I could not read a page giving his findings on landlessness.

The Survey of Palestine and the Village Statistics are cited from copies on palestineremembered.com and the PLO Research Center reprint; those sites are advocacy, so the copies count as government/advocacy. I found no readable copy of the original on a neutral site.
I found no reliable page giving the share of land bought from small owners or peasants; the 9.4 percent figure (Granott) appears on the Lehn paper, which was not readable in the last check.
The public (state) share of Palestine's land: I found only the explanation of what 'public' land included, not a reliable single percentage; the Village Statistics reprint carries the table.
Figures for Jewish-owned land differ (1.49, 1.73, 1.85 and 2.0 million dunams) by date and by whether concessions and undivided shares count; I could not reconcile them from the pages I read.
not_claimed: This card does not say the land was 'empty' or that all sellers were willing; Hope Simpson and Shaw document displacement and fear.
It does not say purchases were illegal; they were legal under the Mandate, and restricted from 1940.
It does not cover the land that changed hands in and after 1948.
It does not say 6.6 percent is the share of cultivable land; the cultivated or cultivable share was higher.
